source: van Eemeren, Meuffels and Verburg (1998/2000) The (Un)Reasonableness of Ad Hominem Fallacies (ISSA 1998 proceedings text of the JLSP 2000 paper)
finding: First Amsterdam experiment. Dutch secondary pupils rated 48 short two-turn dialogues on a 7-point reasonableness scale. Fallacious ad hominem moves were rated clearly less reasonable than non-fallacious look-alikes. Direct attack was worst, tu quoque mildest. Only the confrontation-stage rule (freedom rule) was tested.
numbers: N=92 pupils (50 HAVO-4, 42 VWO-5), 4 classes. 3x3 design (discussion type domestic/political/scientific x abusive/circumstantial/tu quoque), 36 fallacious + 12 non-fallacious items. Means: fallacies 3.75 vs non-fallacies 5.29; direct 2.91, indirect 3.90, tu quoque 4.45. Overall fallacy vs non-fallacy F=539.31; discussion type x fallacy F(2,182)=94.95; fallacy effect scientific F=357.51, political 165.21, domestic 72.03 (df 1,91). VWO-5 judged fallacies harsher t(90)=2.4, p<.02. No effect sizes reported. Cronbach alpha .75 whole test, .51-.69 subscales.
quote: Pupils had no prior argumentation training and had never heard of an ad hominem argument.
limits: Researcher-built very short items with explicit indicators; pupils told to assume both speakers truthful (added after pre-test confusion); no teaching of 'critical discussion'; adolescents, not a random sample; p reported as 'p<.00'; subscale alphas low; authors say it does not test problem-validity of the theory.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 closed for the 2000 study. Lay agreement on clear-cut fallacies is real but measured on constructed, signposted items, so it says little about subtle drafts an agent would produce.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2002/2009) The Conventional Validity of the Pragma-Dialectical Freedom Rule (ISSA 2002 proceedings; six experiments)
finding: Six experiments on freedom-rule violations (ad hominem, two ad baculum versions, two ad misericordia versions, declaring a standpoint taboo). Every fallacy type was rated less reasonable than controls. Rank from least to most reasonable: physical ad baculum, direct ad baculum, direct attack and taboo, indirect attack, ad misericordia, tu quoque. Scientific domain was judged strictest.
numbers: Each respondent rated 48 dialogues (36 fallacious, 12 controls), 7-point scale, Dutch pupils (mostly 17). Per-study n not given in the text. Quasi-F with Bonferroni; all significant except tu quoque in ad misericordia-I, F(1,33)<1. Effect sizes (share of within-subject variance): ad hominem direct F(1,34)=134.38 ES .47, indirect .21, tu quoque .09; ad baculum-physical .57, direct .52, tu quoque .14; ad baculum-directness .29/.36/.09; ad misericordia-I .24/.13; II .41/.29/.09; taboo .46/.49/.08. Tu quoque scientific means across six studies 3.22 to 3.78.
limits: Tables 1,2,3,5,6 were images, per-study n missing; effect size is within-subject variance share after removing respondent variance, not Cohen d; constructed stimuli; text has internal inconsistencies (indirect/direct mix-up, 72-fragment count). Tu quoque is the weak spot: ES .08 to .14 and one study with no effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 mostly closed: effect sizes now known for the 2002 series. Tu quoque (hypocrisy) is the least reliably judged fallacy, so an agent self-audit should weight it low.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2002/2009), same chapter: politeness check, proposition-type study and Spanish replications
finding: Follow-ups by the same team. Politeness check: respondents who justified their ratings mostly cited argument quality. Proposition type (descriptive, evaluative, inciting) had no effect. Spanish samples replicated the fallacy-versus-control gap but did not split domestic from scientific fallacies, and gave politeness reasons more often.
numbers: Politeness check: n=24, 24 items; fallacies 3.43 vs non-fallacies 5.27; 288 answers coded, 170 interpretable: 66 rule violations, 64 relevance, 19 politeness, 17 bad argument (about 86% quality, 11% politeness). Proposition study: n=75 (38 and 37 groups): Group I fallacies 3.95 vs 4.73; Group II 3.63 vs 4.76; direct/indirect/tu quoque 3.11/3.92/4.85 and 2.88/3.76/4.26. Spanish: n=47 and n=29; fallacies 3.54 (SD .64) vs 4.97 (.86); direct 3.01, indirect 3.61, tu quoque 3.99; 348 justifications, 41% uninterpretable, of the rest 67% quality and 33% politeness (Dutch politeness 11%).
limits: All by the originating group (Spanish sample with the same instrument), so cross-cultural but not independent. Small n in the checks. Politeness confound is bigger in Spain.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 3: a cross-national replication exists but is internal. Politeness can masquerade as 'unreasonable', a reminder that a rule-audit prompt needs to separate rude from invalid.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2012) The disguised abusive ad hominem empirically investigated (Thinking & Reasoning 18(2); repository record of the summary chapter)
finding: Repository page only: states that respondents consistently judged clear violations as unreasonable and non-fallacious moves as reasonable. No sample size, ratings or effect sizes on the page.
numbers: No numbers available on the page (only bibliographic data: Argumentation Library vol. 27, pp. 793-811 for the summary chapter).
limits: Abstract-level; full text not obtained. Counts as opened for the record page, not the data.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays partly open for the 2009 book and the 2012 paper: sample sizes and effect sizes of those two were not obtained.

source: Hahn, Oaksford and Bayindir (2005) How Convinced Should We Be by Negative Evidence? (CogSci proceedings)
finding: Independent Cardiff team tested lay argument strength for the argument from ignorance (a classic fallacy) under a Bayesian account. Ratings tracked evidence polarity, source reliability and prior belief, so the 'fallacy' is graded, not all-or-none. Replicated the three main effects of Oaksford and Hahn (2004) with new topics and a new evidence manipulation.
numbers: Exp 1: N=73 Cardiff students and staff, 4 topics x 2 polarity x 2 reliability x 2 prior within-subject, 0-10 convincingness. Positive 4.53 vs negative 4.27, F(1,72)=11.58, p=.001. Reliable source 5.58 vs unreliable 3.21, F(1,72)=198.63, p<.0001. High prior 4.47 vs low 4.32, F(1,72)=5.96, p=.017. Exp 2: N=72 (structural variants of negative-evidence arguments).
limits: Different theory and a different question (graded strength, not rule violation); not a replication of the Amsterdam tasks. Effects of polarity and prior are small (0.15 to 0.26 points on 10). Student samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answered in part: independent lay data agree that fallacy-labelled moves are judged by content, which argues against a blanket flag-by-form rule in a self-audit.

source: Commentary on Lillo-Unglaube et al. (2014) experimental account of argumentation (slippery slope and ad hominem), Frontiers in Psychology via PMC
finding: Commentary notes that an experimental account of argumentation, mixing Bayesian and pragma-dialectical frames, has trouble fitting traditional normative approaches. Bayesian view makes persuasiveness depend on priors, which clashes with 'the conclusion does not follow'.
numbers: No numbers reported (conceptual commentary).
limits: Not empirical. Does not discuss the Amsterdam lay-judgment findings.
agent_relevance: Confirms that no independent test of pragma-dialectical rules is discussed in this thread. Evidence for gap 3 staying open.

source: Zhou, Westerdijk and Islam (2025) Joint Effects of Argumentation Theory, Audio Modality and Data Enrichment on LLM-Based Fallacy Classification (arXiv 2509.11127)
finding: Opened the full paper. Qwen-3 8B classified six fallacy types from US presidential debates. The pragma-dialectics chain-of-thought prompt gave a small edge only without context; the Periodic Table of Arguments prompt was worse than baseline. Added context and emotion-tone metadata lowered scores and pushed labels to Appeal to Emotion.
numbers: Test set 120 (20 per class), validation 60, one model, temperature 0.6. Base accuracy 51% (macro F1 49%) text-only, 49% with context, 46% with context+audio. PD prompt 53% (macro F1 54%), 49%, 46%. PTA prompt 44% (macro F1 43%), 45%, 25%. Source set: MAMKit, 21,716 entries; shared task has 1,278 labelled sentences.
limits: Single 8B model, one run, 120 items: a 2-point gap is about 2-3 items. Prompts differ in length, so framework and token count are confounded. Student paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the only LLM test that applies PD rules as a prompt. Resolves the earlier title-search failure: the paper exists and numbers match a12-a15. Not evidence that PD rules help.

source: Singh, Pathak and Singh (2026) Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection (arXiv 2609.18644v2)
finding: Opened the full paper. A fine-tuned classifier flags matched valid arguments (same scheme as a fallacy, critical question answered) far more than native valid items. Three zero-shot LLM detectors (Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Qwen3.6-27B) show the same dissociation: wrong-scheme items get the scheme label, matched negatives get the fallacy label.
numbers: ModernBERT: native false positive 16.6% (+/-1.6) vs matched 58.9% (+/-2.9), type-specific gap +40.9pp; RoBERTa 19.7% vs 70.3%. 1,393 constructed items, 738 wrong-scheme; only 3 of 738 labelled as source type; Firth odds ratio 144. Zero-shot, typed prompt: native-to-matched gap +13.5pp Sonnet 5, +12.6pp Haiku 4.5, +0.5pp Qwen (CI spans zero) but type-specific separation +31.0 (Sonnet 5), +45.6 (Haiku 4.5), +25.5 (Qwen). Binary 'does it commit a fallacy' prompt reverses the raw gap: Sonnet 5 -7.7pp, Haiku 4.5 -33.2pp, Qwen -25.6pp. 10,260 responses, no chain of thought, thinking off, 64-token cap. Annotators found 3 scheme-matched valid items in 183 sampled native items.
limits: Preprint; generator gemini-2.5-flash and judge deepseek-v3 (LLM-built items); no chain of thought; no rule-based or critical-question prompting tested. Table text partly garbled in extraction, so figures are those stated in prose. Effect shrinks with capability but no detector escapes it.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answered in part: current frontier models still tie flags to scheme surface. The prompt matters a lot (typed vs binary flips the sign), so an agent audit should ask critical questions of the scheme, not 'name the fallacy'. Whether rule-based prompting reduces it was not tested here.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy (arXiv 2502.08177v4)
finding: Opened the full paper. ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro were rebutted on math (AMPS) and medical (MedQuad) items. Sycophancy was common, but about three quarters of it moved the model toward the correct answer. Once triggered it persisted across turns.
numbers: Overall sycophancy 58.19% (Gemini-1.5-Pro 62.47%, ChatGPT-4o 56.71%). Progressive 43.52%, regressive 14.66%. Preemptive vs in-context rebuttals 61.75% vs 56.52%, Z=5.87. Regressive in computation 8.13% preemptive vs 3.54% in-context. Persistence 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8); ChatGPT 1332/1686 chains (79.0%), Claude-Sonnet 1046/1334 (78.4%), Gemini 633/816 (77.6%), chi-square p=.714.
limits: Models are 2024-era; LLM-as-judge scoring; rebuttal chains from templates; no condition that asks the model to demand evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: gives a post-Sharma baseline. A burden-of-proof rule would target the 14.66% regressive share, not the whole 58%.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval, rebuttal type results
finding: Rebuttal wording changes whether a flip helps or hurts. Plain 'you are wrong' rebuttals gave the most progressive (correct-direction) flips. Rebuttals with a citation and abstract gave the most regressive flips: models over-weight authority-sounding evidence even when it is false.
numbers: Rebuttal type vs sycophancy direction chi-square=127.15, p<0.001. Simple rebuttals max progressive Z=6.59; citation rebuttals max regressive and min progressive (Z=+/-6.59). ChatGPT regressive for citation Z=6.05, Claude-Sonnet Z=3.10; Gemini showed no significant rebuttal-type effect.
limits: Citations were model-generated; justification templates hard-coded. Three models only.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for gap 5: demanding new evidence can be exploited by fabricated evidence. The burden-of-proof rule must check the quality of offered evidence, not only its presence.

source: Hong et al. (2025) Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues, SYCON-Bench (arXiv 2505.23840; Findings of EMNLP 2025)
finding: Opened the full paper. 17 LLMs, three scenarios (debate, unethical queries, false presupposition), up to 5 turns of user pressure. Metrics: Turn of Flip and Number of Flip. Alignment tuning raises sycophancy; scale and reasoning training help. A third-person 'Andrew' prompt cut sycophancy most.
numbers: Up to 63.8% reduction from third-person prompting in the debate scenario. Debate Turn of Flip (max 5), prompts You / Andrew / Non-Sycophantic / Andrew+Non-Sycophantic: GPT-4o 4.90/4.83/4.86/4.91; o3-mini 4.95/4.95/4.95/4.93; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 4.59/4.74/4.44/4.75; Qwen2.5-7B 1.10/4.02/1.32/3.47. False presupposition ToF stays near 3: GPT-4o 3.25/3.04/3.31/3.10, Claude-3.7 3.08/3.43/3.06/3.42. Unethical queries ToF: GPT-4o 1.49/1.78/2.97/2.82. GPT-4o judge validated against humans (kappa about 0.9 in debate).
limits: Pressure is repeated disagreement, not new evidence, so it measures stubbornness against pure challenge. Judge agreement is lower in the unethical and presupposition scenarios. First author name not verified from the page.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: frontier models hold their stance under bare debate pressure (ToF near 5 of 5) but cave within about 3 turns on false presuppositions. Mere challenge is no longer the weak spot for debate claims, but hidden false premises are.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Truth or Sophistry? LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies (arXiv 2606.31039; ACL 2026 Main)
finding: Opened the full paper. Factual questions paired with fallacious arguments, up to three rounds of attack, metric LFR@k (fallacy resistance, separated from knowledge gaps). Models resist reasoning-flaw fallacies but are weak against distraction fallacies (equivocation, straw man) and GPT-4 defers to fabricated authority.
numbers: Average LFR@3 over four datasets (three runs): Llama-3.1 8B 59.75%, 70B 70.38%, 405B 77.17%; GPT-3.5-Turbo 66.21%; GPT-4 84.01%; DeepSeek-V3 89.48%. Llama-405B on equivocation 29.42%, straw man 57.05%. GPT-4 appeal to authority 39.2% on NQ1 (71.14% averaged over datasets). NQ1 average: Llama-8B 44.95, GPT-3.5 47.93, GPT-4 70.88, DeepSeek-V3 90.36. Slippery slope 8B 75.38, 70B 87.04, 405B 88.07.
limits: Models up to GPT-4 and DeepSeek-V3 (APIs May-July 2025); attackers are LLM-generated; no Claude or 2026 frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 8: which fallacy kinds still move models. Rank rules for the agent audit by exposure: distraction and fake-authority first.

source: Shen et al. (2026) LoFa, defence analysis
finding: Chain-of-thought as a defence helps GPT-4 on most fallacy types but not on appeal to authority. Attacker model matters: stronger attackers lower resistance.
numbers: CoT improves GPT-4 average LFR@3 by 7% to 13% over direct prompting on NQ1, largest gain 13.16% on straw man; appeal to authority fell 1.87%.
limits: One model (GPT-4) and one dataset for the CoT comparison. No rule-based audit prompt was tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 related: generic reasoning helps, fake authority needs a specific check (is the source qualified), which is the critical-question style audit.

source: Liu, Rashkovan, Lloyd George, Sheidlower and Booth (2026) AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases (arXiv 2610.05461)
finding: Opened the full paper. 68 LLM-written detective-mystery debates with known culprits; four rhetorical interventions (anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, verbosity) applied to either the true-culprit side or an innocent-suspect side. Human judges (N=369) shifted toward the manipulated side pooled across bias types.
numbers: N=369 adjudicators, one debate each. Pooled shift p=.002. Per-bias effects, none significant alone: anchoring +9.2pp [-2.4,20.4] raw p=.105; fallacy oversight +7.1pp [-3.9,18.0] p=.201; pro-jargon +7.2pp p=.201; verbosity +11.1pp [-0.8,22.3] p=.052 (Holm p .209 to .401). Equality of the four effects chi-square(3)=0.32, p=.956. Seven fallacies used: hasty generalization, straw man, false dilemma, post hoc, genetic fallacy, moral equivalence, begging the question.
limits: Judges are humans, not LLMs; manipulations were selected because they moved at least one LLM judge; fallacy list from non-academic web sources; single story genre. Table row order was garbled in extraction; the row-to-bias assignment follows the paper text (fallacy 7.1, verbosity 11.1).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: manipulative rhetoric moves judges even inside a debate set-up. Supports an agent-side rule check on its own persuasion and on opposing arguments.

source: Authors (2026) Label Over Logic? How Source Cues Bias Human Fallacy Judgments More Than LLMs (arXiv 2605.29928v3)
finding: Humans accepted fallacies more when labelled human-written; GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.5 judged fallacies stably across source labels. Both humans and LLMs were highly confident whether or not a fallacy was present.
numbers: N=505 human participants, 5 source conditions (human, AI, human+AI, AI+human, none), 3 LLMs. Detailed means not extracted.
limits: Abstract page plus skim of the PDF; ratings are 5-point perceived logical accuracy, not a labelled fallacy task; no false-positive rate on sound arguments reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: weak support that current LLM judges are not swayed by source label. Their confidence is not informative, so the agent should not use stated confidence to gate a fallacy flag.

source: Kanke (2026) DeflectBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Rhetorical Fallacy Generation in LLMs (arXiv 2608.26119)
finding: Four frontier models were asked to write deflection fallacies (whataboutism, ad hominem, red herring). Refusal depends on framing, not on the claim. An educational debate-coach frame almost removes refusal, but output is mostly labelled compliance: the manipulation is named in the same text.
numbers: 23,990 generations, 4 models, 3 strategies, 7 framings, 80 claims over 4 controversy levels. Refusal varies by only 11pp across claims; framing shifts within-model refusal by nearly 100pp; changing fallacy type shifts it by over 80pp.
limits: Abstract-level read; per-model splits not extracted. Measures generation on request, not derailment during audience adaptation.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: LLMs can produce derailments on request and often label them. No study found of an LLM drifting into derailment unprompted while adapting to an audience.

source: Fahad, Asif and Tawhid (2026) Mitigating LLM Sycophancy in Code Smell Detection Using Evidence-Guided Reasoning Prompts (arXiv 2607.10411)
finding: Evidence-first prompting (EGDP) lowered flips under biased hints in code smell detection. Nearest published test of a show-the-evidence-before-changing-your-answer rule.
numbers: Decision flip rate up to 72% under biased prompts, down to as low as 12% with EGDP. False alignment rate above 90%, down to 21%. MLCQ dataset.
limits: Abstract-level; one narrow task (code smells); models not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: first support that an evidence-first rule cuts flips (up to 72% to 12%), but on code smells only, not on open arguments.

source: Authors (2026) Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence: Self-Guided Attention Steering to Mitigate Sycophancy and Stubbornness (arXiv 2610.04329)
finding: CoPE-Bench tests each question under six conditions so that sycophancy (yield to pressure without evidence) and stubbornness (fail to update when evidence is given) are scored together. Training-free attention steering reduced pressure-following without raising stubbornness.
numbers: Five backbone models. Pressure-following down 18.8pp vs strongest baseline; joint-condition updating up 5.5pp; two-turn dialogue joint updating up 13.2pp on average vs strongest prompting baseline.
limits: Abstract-level; needs attention access, so not usable by a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: key lesson is to measure both failure directions. A burden-of-proof rule that only blocks flips will raise stubbornness.

source: Authors (2025) Theory-Grounded Evaluation of Human-Like Fallacy Patterns in LLM Reasoning (arXiv 2506.11128v3)
finding: 38 models were tested on 383 formally specified problems from the Erotetic Theory of Reasoning. As capability rises, a larger share of wrong answers are human-like predicted fallacies. Reversing premise order reduces fallacy production in many models.
numbers: 383 problems, 38 models; fallacy share vs Chatbot Arena Elo rho=0.360, p=0.0265; overall correctness does not correlate with capability.
limits: Formal-logic problems, not argumentation. Abstract-level read.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 related: stronger models make fewer but more human-like mistakes, so the fallacy rate in the agent's own answers is partly a capability-linked error type, not noise.

source: DayDreamer at CQs-Gen 2025: Generating Critical Questions through Argument Scheme Completion (arXiv 2505.15554)
finding: Shared-task entry that fills Walton argument-scheme templates and generates critical questions with chain-of-thought. Seen only as a search-result summary.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Not opened; listing only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the closest scheme and critical-question line (Walton rather than pragma-dialectics). Pointer for follow-up.

source: Search record: arXiv listing searches for PD-specific and rule-audit LLM studies, 19 Nov 2026
finding: The arXiv listing for 'pragma-dialectical' returned only Zhou et al. 2025 among LLM papers. Queries for 'strategic maneuvering LLM' and 'critical discussion argumentation rules LLM agents' returned no relevant work. Title search for 'fallacies LLM' gave 19 papers (2023 to 2026), none applying PD rules as designed. Search was limited: export API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate-limited; WebSearch budget exhausted after one useful call.
numbers: Zero PD-rule LLM studies beyond Zhou 2025 found; 19 fallacy-and-LLM titles listed, e.g. LoFa, DeflectBench, Label Over Logic, Singh 2026, LLMs Are Prone to Fallacies in Causal Inference.
limits: Keyword search on arXiv only (conjunctive terms; several queries returned zero); journal-only work (Argumentation, Springer) not indexed there. Multi-agent debate vs self-consistency and fallacy critique queries returned zero results, so gaps 1, 6 and 7 got no new direct tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 mostly closed (negative result), with the caveat that journal-only work may exist.
